# OrbitGuard — Beginner's Guide to the Full Pipeline

*A companion study guide to the OrbitGuard PRD, written for someone who knows reinforcement learning but not orbital mechanics or multi-agent RL yet. Read this alongside the main PRD and the Excalidraw architecture file — this document explains; those documents specify.*

---

## The one-sentence version

Fifteen satellites are flying around Earth. Every 60 seconds, each one gets a blurry snapshot of where it and its neighbors probably are, a smart "brain" (trained by trial and error) suggests a move, a strict rulebook double-checks that move before letting it happen, and then everyone actually moves. Repeat, for 6 simulated hours, then start a new random scenario and do it all again — thousands of times — until the brain gets good at this.

That's the whole project. Everything below unpacks every piece of that sentence.

---

## Part 1 — The big picture: three loops, nested inside each other

Before the 12-stage pipeline, it helps to see the scale each piece operates at. There are three loops, one inside the next:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TRAINING RUN                                                     │
│ Repeats until the policy converges (checked on the validation    │
│ split). Network weights are initialized ONCE, right at the start.│
│                                                                    │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ ONE BATCH  (~4,000 steps, many episodes)                  │   │
│  │ Weights are updated here (~10 passes), then this batch    │   │
│  │ is discarded. A new batch begins with the updated policy. │   │
│  │                                                              │   │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │   │
│  │  │ ONE EPISODE  (~360 control steps ≈ 6 sim. hours)  │    │   │
│  │  │ Satellite positions & scenario are freshly         │    │   │
│  │  │ re-seeded at the START of each episode.            │    │   │
│  │  │                                                       │    │   │
│  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐     │    │   │
│  │  │  │ ONE CONTROL STEP — the 12-stage pipeline  │     │    │   │
│  │  │  │ Repeats every 60 simulated seconds.        │     │    │   │
│  │  │  │ Network weights stay FIXED the whole time. │     │    │   │
│  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘     │    │   │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The whole 12-stage pipeline below lives entirely inside the innermost box. It's worth keeping this picture in mind, because it's easy to accidentally assume "the network learns something new every step" — it doesn't. It only learns at the batch boundary.

### Why this isn't like a normal supervised-learning dataset

If you're coming from supervised learning, here's the difference that trips people up:

```
SUPERVISED LEARNING                    PPO / MAPPO (on-policy RL)
────────────────────                   ───────────────────────────
Collect a dataset ONCE                 Current policy
        ↓                                      ↓
Train many epochs                      Generate FRESH rollouts
(same data, reused                     (only from the current
 every time)                            policy — never old data)
        ↓                                      ↓
Deploy, done.                          Update weights (~10 passes)
                                                ↓
                                        Discard the batch
                                                ↓
                                        ↻ repeat with the
                                          now-updated policy
```

MAPPO is **on-policy**: it can only learn from data generated by roughly its *current* self. The moment the weights change, old rollouts describe decisions an outdated version of the policy would have made, so they get thrown away rather than reused. There is never a moment where a finished "training set" sits on disk — the simulator generates unlimited fresh scenarios on demand, forever.

**Seeds mean something different here, too.** A *training seed* (3 per configuration) doesn't pin down one fixed set of satellite positions — it seeds the random-number generator for an *entire training run* (initial weights + the whole stream of randomly-generated scenarios that run will encounter). *Evaluation seeds* (10 per trained model, per test condition) are the ones that pin down specific, fixed, reproducible scenarios — but those are only used at the very end, to test an already-trained policy, never during training itself.

## Part 2 — The pipeline, stage by stage

```
GROUND-TRUTH ORBITAL STATE
            ↓
   Sensor / Uncertainty Model
            ↓
      Agent Belief / Estimate
            ↓
       Orbit Prediction
            ↓
 TCA + Minimum Separation + Risk Proxy
            ↓
      Adaptive Pairwise d_safe
            ↓
      MAPPO / CTDE Policy
            ↓
      Maneuver Intent(s)
            ↓
   Deterministic Δv Mapper
            ↓
  Joint-Action Safety Shield
            ↓
     Approved Joint Δv Set
            ↓
      Orbital Propagator
            ↓
          (repeat)
```

### Stage 1 — Ground-truth orbital state

The exact, true position and velocity of all 15 satellites, right now. Nobody in the system sees this directly except the one part that checks "did an actual collision just happen?" Everyone else — the policy, the shield — only ever works from a *blurry version* of this (next stage).

### Stage 2 — Sensor / Uncertainty Model

Real satellite tracking is never perfect — like reading a street sign through fog. This stage deliberately smudges the ground truth with **Gaussian noise** (the standard "bell curve" kind of randomness) and produces a **covariance**: a "fuzzy circle of maybe" around the estimate. A small fuzzy circle means "confident guess"; a big one means "could be anywhere in here."

This is where **J2** belongs in the story. Earth isn't a perfect ball — it bulges very slightly at the equator because it spins. That small, uneven pull is the single biggest real-world disturbance to a low-Earth orbit — bigger than air drag or the moon's pull at these altitudes — so the physics engine has to include it. "Two-body + J2" means: basic gravity between Earth and one satellite (pretending Earth is a perfect sphere, "two-body"), *plus* this one correction for Earth's actual bulgy shape ("+J2").

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="560" alt="Illustration of Earth's equatorial bulge (J2), showing a perfect sphere compared against Earth's actual slightly oblate shape"></p>

### Stage 3 — Agent Belief / Estimate

Light repackaging, nothing more: take the blurry reading from Stage 2 and reshape it into the exact list of numbers the neural network expects as input. No learning happens here, and — important, since this is a common mix-up — **the network's weights are not touched at all** at this stage. "Belief" is just the *input data*; think of the network as a fixed calculator at this point, and belief as the number you type into it.

### Stage 4 — Orbit Prediction

The physics engine runs forward in *simulated* time — not to see what's happening now, but to forecast the next 30 minutes (the **lookahead window**). It uses **RK4 integration** ("Runge-Kutta, 4th order") — a standard way to predict motion accurately, similar to checking your speed and direction several times over the next few seconds instead of assuming you'll walk in a dead-straight line forever.

**A word of caution:** "propagation" here means *orbit* propagation (physics), completely unrelated to "forward propagation" in neural networks (passing data through layers). Same word, two unrelated meanings — the network isn't involved in this stage at all.

Also worth noting: this prediction starts from the *belief*, not the ground truth. If the belief is off, the prediction inherits that error — which is exactly why uncertainty matters so much downstream.

### Stage 5 — TCA, Minimum Separation, and Risk Proxy

For every **pair** of satellites (not each one individually), the system computes:
- **TCA** ("time of closest approach") — when will this pair be nearest each other?
- **Minimum separation** (or "miss distance") — how close will that actually be?

Then it converts that distance, combined with how uncertain both satellites are, into a single **risk proxy** between 0 and 1. Not a light switch (safe/unsafe) — more like a dimmer switch that gradually brightens as things get more dangerous:

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="560" alt="Chart of the risk proxy sigmoid curve, showing risk near 1 at small separation and near 0 at large separation, crossing 0.5 at z=3"></p>

Read the x-axis as "how many uncertainty-widths apart are they?" 0 means right on top of each other relative to how confident we are; 6 means comfortably far apart relative to that same uncertainty. Risk crosses exactly 0.5 at `z0 = 3.0` — "call it a coin-flip level of danger once they're about 3 uncertainty-widths apart."

### Stage 6 — Adaptive Pairwise d_safe

The novel piece of this whole project: instead of one fixed "stay X meters apart" rule, the required safety distance for each pair **stretches or shrinks** based on current uncertainty, local crowding, and risk — always kept between 200 m and 5,000 m. Same instinct as leaving more following distance behind a car in fog than on a clear day: "close" means something different depending on how well you can actually see.

### Stage 7 — MAPPO / CTDE Policy — the actual brain

The only stage in the whole pipeline that's *learned* rather than calculated by a fixed formula. Every RL term in play, unpacked:

| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| **MARL** | The general category: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning — more than one agent learning at once. |
| **MAPPO** | The specific algorithm used: "PPO, extended for multiple agents." |
| **Actor** | The network that actually picks actions — the "player." |
| **Critic** | A training-only "coach" network that estimates how good a situation is, to help the Actor learn faster. Thrown away once training finishes. |
| **Parameter sharing** | All 15 satellites use one identical copy of the Actor's "playbook" — not 15 separate brains. |
| **CTDE** | *Centralized Training, Decentralized Execution.* During practice, the Critic-coach sees the whole constellation. During the real game (and always, once deployed), each satellite only sees its own local view. |
| **POMDP** | *Partially Observable Markov Decision Process* — the formal name for "the agent never sees the true state, only a noisy belief of it." |
| **State / Observation** | Own belief + the 4 most threatening neighbors' info + a small global summary. |
| **Action** | One of the 6 maneuver intents. |
| **Reward** | A score after each move: safety + staying on-mission + not wasting fuel − making the whole group's situation worse. |
| **Discount factor (γ = 0.99)** | How much to care about risk 10 minutes from now vs. right this second. Close to 1 = care almost as much about the near future as right now. |
| **Return** | Total discounted reward added up across a whole episode. |
| **Episode / rollout / trajectory** | One full run: 6 simulated hours, ~360 steps, fresh random start. |
| **On-policy** | Can only learn from data generated by roughly its own current self (see Part 1). |
| **Entropy bonus** | A small nudge during training that discourages locking onto one answer too early — keeps exploring a bit longer. |

### Stage 8 — Maneuver Intent

The Actor's raw output: just a label — `NO_MANEUVER`, `RAISE_ORBIT`, `LOWER_ORBIT`, `PHASE_FORWARD`, `PHASE_BACKWARD`, or `RADIAL_ADJUSTMENT`. Not a real physical push yet — like saying "turn left" before the wheel has actually moved.

### Stage 9 — Deterministic Δv Mapper

**Δv** ("delta-v") is the standard term for "how much you change your velocity" — the actual physical push. This stage is a fixed, non-learned lookup table that turns the Stage-8 label into a real push described in the **RTN frame**: a set of directions that move *with* the satellite, rather than a fixed grid in space — like "forward," "sideways," "up" relative to where you're standing, instead of GPS coordinates.

<p align="center"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="560" alt="Diagram of the RTN local maneuver frame showing R (radial, away from Earth), T (transverse, direction of motion), and N (normal, out of the orbital plane)"></p>

- **R** points straight away from Earth's center (a +R burn pushes the satellite outward).
- **T** points in the direction the satellite is currently moving (a +T burn speeds it up, which — counterintuitively — *raises* the orbit over time).
- **N** points perpendicular to the entire orbital plane — straight "out of the page" if you're looking at the orbit edge-on.

`RAISE_ORBIT` / `LOWER_ORBIT` push hard along T (full magnitude, ±0.1 m/s); `PHASE_FORWARD` / `PHASE_BACKWARD` push gently along that same T axis (half magnitude) for a smaller, more surgical drift adjustment; `RADIAL_ADJUSTMENT` pushes along R for an immediate, non-secular separation change.

### Stages 10–11 — Joint-Action Safety Shield → Approved Δv Set

The strict, non-learned rulebook. It runs in order:

1. **Capability check** — does each proposed Δv fit the satellite's budget, per-action limit, and is maneuvering even enabled for it?
2. **Simulate the consequences** — run the physics forward over the 30-minute lookahead for the surviving joint set of Δv vectors.
3. **Safety checks** — on those simulated results: any actual collisions? Any pair inside its `d_safe`? Any *new* conjunction created, or an existing one made worse? Any satellite deviating too far from its intended orbit?
4. **If everything passes:** approve the whole joint set as-is.
5. **If something fails:** don't throw out everyone's maneuver — only touch the specific satellites actually involved. If 4 or fewer are involved, brute-force try every combination of their 6 possible actions (up to 1,296 combinations — fast) and keep whichever minimizes total risk. If more than 4 are tangled together, brute force gets too expensive, so it switches to **beam search** — a smarter, bounded search that only keeps the 50 most promising partial solutions at each step instead of trying everything.

`NO_MANEUVER` only gets picked for a satellite when the search actually determines that's its *safest* option — never as a default fallback when something gets rejected. "**Approved Δv set**" is simply the *output* of this process, not a separate decision stage on top of it.

### Stage 12 — Orbital Propagator

The physics engine (same RK4 + two-body + J2 from Stage 4) physically applies the approved pushes and advances every satellite's *true* position forward. This becomes the new ground truth, and the whole 12-stage loop repeats — 360 times per episode, thousands of episodes per training run.

*(Note: the visualization/replay UI reads and displays this updated state afterward — it's a separate, optional layer, not part of the physics loop itself. Training runs happen with no visualization involved at all.)*

## Part 3 — Full glossary

### Reinforcement learning

| Term | Plain meaning | Value (current OrbitGuard setup) |
|---|---|---|
| State / Observation | What the agent sees before deciding | Own state + top 4 threat-ranked neighbors + global summary (`k_neighbors = 4`) |
| Action | What the agent can choose to do | 6 discrete intents: `NO_MANEUVER`, `RAISE_ORBIT`, `LOWER_ORBIT`, `PHASE_FORWARD`, `PHASE_BACKWARD`, `RADIAL_ADJUSTMENT` |
| Reward | Feedback score after acting | `R = 1.0·R_safety + 0.3·R_mission − 0.1·‖Δv‖ − 0.5·C_coordination`; collision penalty = −100 |
| Discount factor (γ) | How much future reward matters vs. right now | 0.99 |
| Return | Total reward added up over an episode | N/A — computed per episode, not a set parameter |
| Policy | The strategy — here, the Actor network | Shared Actor network, hidden layers [128, 128] |
| Value function | The Critic's guess at "how good is this situation" | Critic network, hidden layers [256, 256], training-only |
| Actor | The network that actually picks actions | Hidden layers [128, 128], parameter-shared across all 15 satellites |
| Critic | The training-only coach network | Hidden layers [256, 256], centralized inputs (all agents' states/risks) |
| Parameter sharing | One shared brain for every agent | Enabled — 1 network for N = 15 satellites |
| CTDE | Full info during training, local-only info when acting | N/A — architectural pattern, not a numeric setting |
| MARL | The general category: RL with multiple agents | N/A — category name, not a parameter |
| MAPPO | The specific algorithm: multi-agent PPO | `learning_rate=3e-4`, `clip_param=0.2`, `gae_lambda=0.95`, `train_batch_size=4000`, `sgd_minibatch_size=256`, `num_sgd_iter=10` |
| POMDP | "The agent never sees the true state, only a belief" | N/A — formal framework, not a parameter |
| On-policy | Can only learn from data its current self generated | N/A — property of the algorithm, not a set value |
| Episode / rollout / trajectory | One full run from start to finish | `episode_horizon=21,600s` (6h) ÷ `control_dt=60s` = 360 steps/episode |
| Entropy bonus | Nudges the policy to keep exploring, not lock in early | `entropy_coeff = 0.01` |

### Orbital mechanics & physics

| Term | Plain meaning | Value (current OrbitGuard setup) |
|---|---|---|
| Two-body problem | Gravity between just Earth and one satellite, nothing else | Combined with J2 in the dynamics model (`dynamics.model = two_body_j2`) |
| J2 | Earth's slight equatorial bulge — the biggest real perturbation | Included in `dynamics.model = two_body_j2` |
| RK4 | A standard, accurate way to predict motion step by step | Integrator: RK4, `physics_dt = 10s` |
| TLE | The standard published format for describing a real orbit | Frozen CelesTrak Starlink-shell snapshot, pulled once at Week 1 |
| RTN frame | Local directions: R (outward), T (along motion), N (sideways out of plane) | N/A — coordinate system definition, not a numeric setting |
| Δv (delta-v) | How much a maneuver changes velocity | `base_delta_v=0.1 m/s` (full), `0.05 m/s` (phase, half); budget `remaining_delta_v=2.0 m/s` |
| TCA | The predicted moment two objects are closest | Computed over `lookahead=1,800s` (30 min) window |
| Minimum separation / miss distance | How close that closest moment actually is | N/A — a computed output per pair, not a fixed parameter |
| Hard-body radius | The physical size used to define an actual collision | `5m` per satellite (`10m` combined for a typical pair) |

### System & safety design

| Term | Plain meaning | Value (current OrbitGuard setup) |
|---|---|---|
| Ground truth | The exact, true state — never shown to the policy | N/A — concept, not a numeric setting |
| Uncertainty / covariance | How wrong an estimate might be — a "fuzzy circle of maybe" | `σ_pos=100m` (1σ/axis), `σ_vel=0.1 m/s` (1σ/axis) |
| Belief | The noisy estimate, reshaped for the network | `covariance_mode = true_estimate` (MVP simplification) |
| Adaptive safety margin (`d_safe`) | Required distance that stretches/shrinks with conditions | `d_base=1000m`, `d_min=200m`, `d_max=5000m`, `α=1.0`, `β=0.5`, `γ=1.0` |
| Risk proxy | A 0–1 danger score, not a hard threshold | `z0=3.0`, `k=1.5`, `ε=1.0m` |
| Deterministic | Same input always gives the same output — no learning involved | N/A — a property/description, not a value |
| Joint-action shield | Checks everyone's moves together, not one at a time | Exact search ≤4 affected agents, else beam search |
| Beam search | "Keep only the most promising few options" when there are too many to check all of | `beam_width = 50` |
| Distribution shift | Testing under conditions the policy never trained on | 4 core scenarios: noise ↑, density ↑ (N fixed), simultaneous conjunctions, capability ↓ |
| Baseline / ablation | A comparison version of the system, used to prove what actually helped | 5 baselines: No-Maneuver, Rule-Based, Fixed-Margin MAPPO, Adaptive MAPPO, Adaptive MAPPO (no shield) |
| Seed | A fixed starting point for randomness, used for reproducibility | 3 training seeds/config · 10 evaluation seeds/model |

## Part 4 — What to learn, in order

Starting point assumed: you know RL fundamentals (states, actions, rewards, policies, value functions) from a standard course, but not much beyond that.

1. **Actor-critic methods → PPO specifically** — the clipped objective, why it stabilizes training, generalized advantage estimation (GAE).
2. **Multi-agent RL** — CTDE, parameter sharing, why multi-agent training is harder (the environment looks non-stationary since everyone else is also learning at once).
3. **POMDPs** — the formal framework for "the agent doesn't see the true state."
4. **Safe / shielded RL** — wrapping a learned policy with a non-learned safety checker is its own small subfield, worth a couple of papers before implementing the shield.
5. **Orbital mechanics basics** — the two-body problem, Keplerian elements (semi-major axis, eccentricity, inclination), J2, the RTN frame, what a TLE is.
6. **Numerical integration** — RK4, standard applied math, nothing space-specific.
7. **Probability** — Gaussian distributions and covariance, since uncertainty feeds both the risk formula and the adaptive margin formula.
8. **ML methodology** — train/validation/test separation, why you fix seeds, paired statistical comparison, what an ablation study is.
9. **Tooling** — PettingZoo (multi-agent environment API) and RLlib (training library); the concepts aren't hard, but wiring a custom environment correctly takes real time.
